sentences.text: He told his mother in November and it went about as well as these things go, which is to say she was kind and completely missed it.
She said everybody found moving hard.
She said it took a year.

She said she had been miserable too when she was thirteen and Granny had moved them to Aberdeen, and that it had come good, and that he was doing so well and that Miss Cameron had said he was settling in beautifully.
All of which was true, and none of which was the thing.
He tried Mr Ross, obliquely, at the end of a Thursday, on the pretext of asking about local stories for a project he had not been set.
Mr Ross was about sixty and had been at that school for twenty-eight years and was not in a hurry.
He taught history to three year groups and ran the minibus and had a way of answering a question about forty seconds after you had given up on him.

He listened to the whole of Tam's very careful question about the fox — a question that mentioned folklore twice and did not mention Tam at all — and then he sat back and said, "How often are you seeing it?" Tam looked at the desk.
"Most days," he said.
"Aye," said Mr Ross, and did not seem surprised, and did not say anything for a bit.
"The rule's about the wood," Tam said.
"That's what everybody says.
In the wood, off the path, don't know where the road is." "That's what everybody says because that's where everybody's seen it, once, when they were eleven and daft." Mr Ross took his glasses off.
"It's not a rule about woods, son.
It's a rule about not knowing where you are." Tam said nothing for a moment.

"That's the same thing." "It is not remotely the same thing," said Mr Ross, "and you know fine it isn't, or you wouldn't have come in here with a project you've not been set." "I know where I am." "Do you." Tam did not answer that.

"I've been here twenty-eight years," said Mr Ross, "and I came from Glasgow, and I saw that animal roughly every second day for the whole of my first winter, and I have not seen it since about 1999." Tam sat there.
"Nobody else says that," he said.
"Everybody says once.
Everybody says they saw it once, off the path, when they were wee." "Aye.
Because everybody here got lost in a wood once when they were wee and found their way out by teatime." Mr Ross put his glasses back on.
"You cannot be lost in a place you were born in.
It is not available to you.
Which is why the folk in this village think it's a story about a wood — because for them, it is." He started stacking papers, which meant the conversation had about ninety seconds left.
"There's maybe four people in Fernaig it's not a story about a wood for.
I'm one.

You're one." "Who are the other two?" "That," said Mr Ross, "would be their business." "What changed?" "I stopped pretending I was fine," said Mr Ross, "which took me thirteen months and a very bad Christmas, and I would not particularly recommend the method."
